newsitem.title: GERMANY: M3, steady repo rate kill talk of early Buba hike.
newsitem.headline: M3, steady repo rate kill talk of early Buba hike.

text.p: The Bundesbank kept its main money market rate at 3.00 percent on Tuesday and killed off talk of an imminent interest rate rise by announcing a sharp slowdown in M3 money supply growth, its key policy guide.
As expected, the bank set its auction for securities repurchase agreements, or repos, at a fixed 3.00 percent this week, the rate that has prevailed for the past year.

M3 growth, seen by the Bundesbank as a reliable indicator of future inflation, slowed to an annualised rate of 5.7 percent in July from 6.4 percent in June. The rate was well below economists' forecasts which had averaged 6.3 percent.
The news convinced financial markets the Bundesbank is most unlikely to raise key interest rates when it its council meets on Thursday for the first time after a four-week summer break.
"This is very nice for the Bundesbank because it means they can hold off on an interest rate move for the time being," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.
"They can have a relaxed Bundesbank meeting on Thursday."

The dollar strengthened against the mark to test 1.84 marks after the M3 data but fell back to 1.8350 marks by 1200 GMT. German government bond futures also firmed, with the September contract on 10-year Bunds up eight basis points at 102.68.

Tuesday's M3 news coincided with an upbeat assessment from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) which said the Bundesbank was unlikely to change its policy stance up until the end of 1998, when it will hand monetary policy to the European Central Bank.

Robert Price, director of OECD countries division, said: "At this time we see no reason for a change in monetary policy." He added however, "That does not mean that the Bundesbank might not see the necessity to change its policy."
But many economists expect a repo rate rise in the coming months, with forecasts varying from a rate of 3.20 to 3.50 percent by end-1997.

Several senior Bundesbank officials have fanned fears of a rate rise in recent weeks by saying they are concerned about the speed of the mark's depreciation this year and about signs of inflationary pressures in the pipeline.

Economists say a slight uptick in consumer inflation to two percent or 2.1 percent in the autumn from 1.9 percent in July, and further signs of an acceleration in economic growth, could provide the Bundesbank with the justification for a rate rise.
"All in all, the price environment has clouded, not only due to the weaker mark, but also for domestic reasons," analysts Trinkaus & Burkhardt wrote in a note to investors.

Even though M3 growth has been within the Bundesbank's 1997 target corridor of 3-1/2 percent to 6-1/2 percent for the past two months, it remains above its five percent target level for 1997 and 1998.
And M3 could rise towards the end of this year if tax revenue shortfalls force the government to step up borrowing.
Meanwhile economists polled by Reuters on Tuesday unanimously predicted the Bundesbank will keep interest rates unchanged on Thursday and set next week's repo auction at 3.00 percent as well.

Three of 10 analysts polled said they expected a rise in the Bundesbank's 2.50 percent discount and 4.50 percent Lombard rates this year while three expect it to switch to variable-rate repo auctions this year -- a move that would signal higher money market rates.
The July fall in M3 growth was caused by a slowdown in lending to the private sector and a pick-up in investment in bonds, the Bundesbank said.
Alison Cottrell at Painewebber noted that the Bundesbank's positive comments about M3 indicated that it was not yet seeking justification for a rate move.
"If they wanted to do some tightening on rates, they would have set up the domestic justification," Cottrell said. "It was reassuring in that sense."
The Bundesbank added that public sector demand for credit and net fund inflows from domestic non-banks' foreign transactions continued to have an "expansive" effect on the money supply.
